government.name: City of Surrey
government.howBuilt: This list draws on reporting from 2026 Surrey mayoral forums and campaign coverage in local news, candidate profiles published by the City of Surrey, and candidate questionnaires published by the Surrey Now-Leader. We kept issues the City of Surrey can act on through its budget, zoning, bylaws, policing budget, city facilities, and its votes on the regional district. Issues mainly run by the province, such as health care and school funding, are left out, and rapid transit is included only where the city lobbies for it.

issues.title: Public safety and policing
issues.description: How the city responds to crime, including extortion targeting local businesses, gang violence, and property crime.
issues.whatItAffects: Residents, business owners, and the size and cost of the Surrey Police Service, fire service, and bylaw teams.
issues.whoDecides: Council approves the police, fire, and bylaw budgets each year and decides how much to spend on officers, equipment, and prevention programs.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city grow its public safety spending?
viewQuestion.poleA: Hire many more police officers and add enforcement tools quickly
viewQuestion.poleB: Grow policing gradually and fund prevention and other services alongside it

tradeoffs.context: Safety spending competes with other services, so faster growth in policing usually means higher taxes or less for other programs.

gains: More officers could respond faster to calls and investigate more cases
A visible enforcement push may reassure residents and business owners
costs: Rapid police growth may raise property taxes or squeeze other services
Enforcement alone may not address the causes behind some crime

gains: Prevention programs may reduce some crime before it happens
Slower growth may keep tax increases smaller and more predictable
costs: Police response times and staffing may improve more slowly
Some residents may feel the city is not acting fast enough

issues.title: Property taxes and city spending
issues.description: How much the city raises through property taxes, parcel taxes, and fees, and what that money pays for.
issues.whatItAffects: Homeowners, renters through their rent, businesses, and everyone who uses city services.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets the annual budget, property tax rate, parcel taxes, and user fees, and decides which services and projects to fund or delay.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city balance its budget?
viewQuestion.poleA: Freeze or cut taxes, even if some services or projects wait
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep investing in services and projects, even if taxes rise

tradeoffs.context: A growing city needs more services, so holding taxes down usually means slowing or cutting some spending.

gains: Households and businesses would face smaller or no tax increases
Pressure to find savings may lead to closer review of spending
costs: Some projects, services, or staffing may be delayed or reduced
Costs may shift to user fees or build up as future repairs

gains: Services and facilities could keep pace with population growth
Infrastructure may be maintained before problems become costly
costs: Tax bills would rise, adding to household and business costs
Higher taxes may weigh most on people with fixed or lower incomes

issues.title: City Centre arena and entertainment district
issues.description: Whether to go ahead with the planned 10,000-seat arena, hotel, and entertainment district on King George Boulevard in City Centre.
issues.whatItAffects: City finances, City Centre development, events and sports, and what other facilities the city can afford.
issues.whoDecides: Council approves the city's land deals, funding, and contracts for the arena project, and can change or review them.

viewQuestion.question: What should the city do with the arena project?
viewQuestion.poleA: Proceed with the planned arena and entertainment district
viewQuestion.poleB: Stop or rework the arena deal and spend the money elsewhere

tradeoffs.context: The arena is a large, long-term commitment, so the choice weighs a major City Centre attraction against other uses for the money.

gains: City Centre could gain a large events venue, hotel, and new activity
Signed contracts and planning work would not be reopened
costs: The city may carry construction and operating cost risks
Money and staff time may be less available for other facilities

gains: Funds could go to pools, rinks, fields, or other priorities
The city may avoid some long-term financial risk
costs: Ending or changing signed agreements may carry its own costs
City Centre may wait longer for a large gathering venue

issues.title: Housing supply and growth
issues.description: How quickly new homes get approved and built in Surrey, what kinds, and how affordable they are.
issues.whatItAffects: Renters, first-time buyers, families, and neighbourhoods facing new development.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets zoning, approves rezonings and permits, sets development charges, and can set permit timelines and some local housing taxes.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city approach new housing?
viewQuestion.poleA: Approve more homes faster, including denser buildings near transit
viewQuestion.poleB: Grow more gradually and match growth to roads, schools, and services

tradeoffs.context: Housing choices often trade how fast new homes arrive against how well roads, schools, and services keep up.

gains: More homes could be built sooner, easing pressure on rents and prices
Faster permits may lower costs for builders and buyers
costs: Infrastructure and schools may fall behind new population
Neighbourhoods may see more traffic and change

gains: Roads, schools, and amenities may better keep pace with growth
Neighbourhoods may change more gradually
costs: Fewer new homes could keep prices and rents higher for longer
People may wait longer for the housing types they need

issues.title: Homelessness and supportive housing
issues.description: How the city responds to people without homes, including shelters, supportive housing sites, and use of public spaces.
issues.whatItAffects: People who are unhoused, nearby residents and businesses, and users of parks and sidewalks.
issues.whoDecides: Council approves sites and zoning for shelters and supportive housing, sets rules for public spaces, and partners with BC Housing and health agencies.

viewQuestion.question: What should the city focus on?
viewQuestion.poleA: Approve more shelter and supportive housing sites across the city
viewQuestion.poleB: Focus on enforcing rules in public spaces and limiting new sites

tradeoffs.context: Cities often weigh adding housing and services for unhoused people against concerns about public spaces and nearby impacts.

gains: More people could move indoors and get connected to services
Fewer people may need to shelter in parks and on streets
costs: Some neighbours may object to new sites near them
The city depends on provincial partners to fund and run sites

gains: Parks and sidewalks may be kept clearer for general use
Nearby residents and businesses may see fewer impacts
costs: People may be displaced without a place to go
Enforcement may move problems elsewhere rather than resolve them

issues.title: Transportation and transit
issues.description: How people get around Surrey, including roads, sidewalks, congestion, and the city's push for rapid transit.
issues.whatItAffects: Commuters, drivers, transit riders, pedestrians, and neighbourhoods along major corridors.
issues.whoDecides: Council builds and maintains city roads and sidewalks and lobbies TransLink and the province, which fund and run rapid transit.

viewQuestion.question: Where should the city focus its transportation push?
viewQuestion.poleA: Push for new SkyTrain lines on major corridors like King George
viewQuestion.poleB: Focus on bus rapid transit and local road and sidewalk upgrades

tradeoffs.context: Big rapid transit lines take years and outside funding, while smaller projects can arrive sooner but carry fewer riders.

gains: SkyTrain could move many people quickly over the long term
Rapid transit may support new homes and jobs along the line
costs: Lines depend on provincial and federal funding and take years
City effort may shift away from nearer-term local fixes

gains: Bus lanes, roads, and sidewalks could improve sooner
Costs are lower and more within the city's own control
costs: Buses may carry fewer people than a SkyTrain line
Busy corridors may still face congestion over time

issues.title: Metro Vancouver regional costs
issues.description: Surrey's role in the Metro Vancouver regional district, which runs water, sewer, and garbage systems and charges member cities.
issues.whatItAffects: Utility bills, regional sewer and water projects, and regional parks and planning.
issues.whoDecides: Council appoints Surrey's regional directors, votes on regional budgets, and can press for changes or seek to withdraw from some services.

viewQuestion.question: How should Surrey approach Metro Vancouver?
viewQuestion.poleA: Pull back from regional services other than core utilities
viewQuestion.poleB: Stay in fully and push for reforms from the inside

tradeoffs.context: Regional services share costs across cities, so leaving some trades shared savings for more local control.

gains: Surrey could control more of its own services and spending
Residents may pay less toward regional programs outside Surrey
costs: The city may need to fund or build replacement services itself
Leaving could strain relations with neighbouring cities

gains: Surrey keeps a voice in shared regional decisions
Costs of parks, planning, and services stay shared
costs: Reforms may be slow and depend on other cities agreeing
Surrey may keep paying toward projects outside its borders

issues.title: Recreation and community facilities
issues.description: Building and running pools, rinks, community centres, sports fields, and parks across Surrey's neighbourhoods.
issues.whatItAffects: Families, youth, seniors, sports groups, and neighbourhoods that lack nearby facilities.
issues.whoDecides: Council decides which facilities to build, where, and when, and how to pay for them through taxes, borrowing, or development charges.

viewQuestion.question: How quickly should the city build new facilities?
viewQuestion.poleA: Build new pools, rinks, and community centres soon
viewQuestion.poleB: Pace new facilities to limit borrowing and tax increases

tradeoffs.context: New facilities serve a growing population but come with construction and long-term operating costs.

gains: Growing neighbourhoods could get nearby pools, rinks, and centres
Shorter waitlists for programs and sports
costs: Borrowing and operating costs may raise taxes or fees
Other projects may be delayed to pay for them

gains: Debt and tax increases may stay lower
Each project may get more time for planning and cost control
costs: Facilities may stay crowded as population grows
Some neighbourhoods may wait years for nearby amenities

issues.title: City Hall accountability and oversight
issues.description: How closely city spending, land deals, and decisions are reviewed and reported to the public.
issues.whatItAffects: How taxpayers' money is tracked, how open council decisions are, and how much staff time goes to reviews.
issues.whoDecides: Council can order audits, create oversight offices, and set rules for transparency and public reporting.

viewQuestion.question: Does City Hall need more outside oversight?
viewQuestion.poleA: Add independent audits and new oversight of city spending
viewQuestion.poleB: Rely on existing audits and council review to oversee spending

tradeoffs.context: More oversight can build public trust, but reviews also take time and money.

gains: Residents may get clearer information on spending and deals
Independent reviewers could catch problems earlier
costs: New audits and offices add their own costs
Reviews may slow some decisions and projects

gains: Staff and money stay focused on delivering services
Decisions may move ahead without added delays
costs: Some residents may remain doubtful about city spending
Problems may surface later than they would with outside review

election.name: City of Surrey general local election
election.howToVote: Eligible City of Surrey voters can vote at any of 52 voting places on General Voting Day (Saturday, Oct. 17, 8 a.m.-8 p.m.) or at any of 10 advance voting places on Oct. 7, 10, 14 or 15. Registered voters should bring their voter card and one piece of acceptable ID. Voters who are not registered can register at the voting place with two pieces of acceptable ID; non-resident property electors must register in advance.
election.voteByMail: Voters can request a mail ballot package until Oct. 14, 2026; completed ballots must be received by 8 p.m. on Oct. 17 by mail, at City Hall, or in the after-hours drop boxes.

notes:
surrey.patch-1.json: Main sources: City of Surrey candidate profiles (bios, official_guide) and Surrey Now-Leader 'Meet your Surrey candidates' questionnaires (news). Leanna Chatwin (New Surrey+) submitted no bio; her positions come from the New Surrey+ slate's group questionnaire answers, so summary is null. Philip Carless says he is running as an independent (city profile and Now-Leader); declaredIndependent may be set true. Isaac Daniel and Intikhab Ahmed are listed as independents by the Now-Leader. Mike Bose arena vote from city-released vote count (only Annis and Bose opposed); the same record implies other sitting councillors including Harry Bains voted in favour, but attendance isn't listed, so no position was added for Bains. Social links use only handles shown on the official profile; conflicting handles (Alexis, Bajwa) were left out. Dan B. Carlos's priority on transparency of educational materials was left out as a school-board matter. No blocked pages.
surrey.patch-2.json: Affiliations unchanged (already verified in base). surrey.iandehoog.com blocked (robots fetch timeout); safesurreycoalition.ca/platform failed (too many redirects), so Safe Surrey platform items cite the homepage. surreynow.ca homepage returned no content (no Surrey NOW platform used). New Surrey+ has no website/platform found. Nothing found for Messia Ditshimba or Christopher R. Hoffmann (official profiles list only contact info; no news). Emily Kennedy: only official profile statement. No Now-Leader profiles for Dunn, Ditshimba, Hoffmann, Kennedy. Meera Gill hospital-site position is issueId null (city land/permits for a provincial facility). Surrey Connect platform cited via its linked PDF.
surrey.patch-3.json: All 17 assigned candidates checked on surrey.ca profiles and Surrey Now-Leader 'Meet your candidates' Q&As (Oct 4, 2026). matthew-j-smed: surrey.ca profile has contact info only; no Now-Leader Q&A, no New Surrey+ website, no news found - positions empty. tom-said did not answer the Now-Leader questionnaire; positions from surrey.ca statement. jimmy-rico: surrey.ca statement only. safesurreycoalition.ca/platform failed (too many redirects); used homepage platform list. surreynow.ca returned no platform text (JS-rendered), so no Surrey NOW slate items used. Several items (hospital, health care, food, supervised consumption sites) are provincial or off-scale and given issueId null. allison-patton: surrey.ca calls her a former councillor (base incumbent:false is consistent). Pullar's gender is described inconsistently across sources; summaries avoid pronouns. Social links built from handles printed on surrey.ca/Now-Leader pages.
surrey.patch-4.json: Sources: City of Surrey candidate profiles (official_guide) and Surrey Now-Leader 'Meet your Surrey candidates' questionnaires (news), plus slate platforms (Surrey First our-vision page/home page, Surrey Connect platform PDF, Conservative surreyconservatives.com/platform, Imagine Surrey /vision/). Miguel Ting declined the Now-Leader questionnaire and his city profile has no policy statements: positions []. James Yu: no city bio and Now-Leader received no questionnaire; positions use Surrey NOW slate pillars reported by The Times of Canada (surreynow.ca is script-rendered, no readable platform). Lily Tsi and Grace Zeigler (New Surrey+) have no personal policy statements; positions come from the New Surrey+ group answer in the Now-Leader (which spells her 'Ziegler'; the city list uses 'Zeigler'). Tsi has no bio. Affiliations left unchanged (base values match the city profiles). Surrey Connect profiles list affiliation as 'Surrey Connect Public IA'; Conservative profiles show 'Conservative' and the Now-Leader calls it 'Conservative Party of Surrey' - base uses the official list names. Social links only where the city profile shows a handle; Donna Wu's X handle left out. Surrey First platform 300-officer figure is from the home page; the vision page has no number. No blocked pages.
